topics.title: Rates of reaction and energy changes

refs.1.1: Describe how the Dalton model of an atom has changed over time because of the discovery of subatomic particles
refs.1.2: Describe the structure of an atom as a nucleus containing protons and neutrons, surrounded by electrons in shells
refs.1.3: Recall the relative charge and relative mass of: a a proton b a neutron c an electron
refs.1.4: Explain why atoms contain equal numbers of protons and electrons
refs.1.5: Describe the nucleus of an atom as very small compared to the overall size of the atom
refs.1.6: Recall that most of the mass of an atom is concentrated in the nucleus
refs.1.7: Recall the meaning of the term mass number of an atom
refs.1.8: Describe atoms of a given element as having the same number of protons in the nucleus and that this number is unique to that element
refs.1.9: Describe isotopes as different atoms of the same element containing the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons in their nuclei
refs.1.10: Calculate the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in atoms given the atomic number and mass number
refs.1.11: Explain how the existence of isotopes results in relative atomic masses of some elements not being whole numbers
refs.1.12: Calculate the relative atomic mass of an element from the relative masses and abundances of its isotopes
refs.1.13: Describe how Dmitri Mendeleev arranged the elements, known at that time, in a periodic table by using properties of these elements and their compounds
refs.1.14: Describe how Dmitri Mendeleev used his table to predict the existence and properties of some elements not then discovered
refs.1.15: Explain that Dmitri Mendeleev thought he had arranged elements in order of increasing relative atomic mass but this was not always true because of the relative abundance of isotopes of some pairs of elements in the periodic table
refs.1.16: Explain the meaning of atomic number of an element in terms of position in the periodic table and number of protons in the nucleus
refs.1.17: Describe that in the periodic table a elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic number, in rows called periods b elements with similar properties are placed in the same vertical columns called groups
refs.1.18: Identify elements as metals or non-metals according to their position in the periodic table, explaining this division in terms of the atomic structures of the elements
refs.1.19: Predict the electronic configurations of the first 20 elements in the periodic table as diagrams and in the form, for example 2.8.1
refs.1.20: Explain how the electronic configuration of an element is related to its position in the periodic table
refs.1.21: Explain how ionic bonds are formed by the transfer of electrons between atoms to produce cations and anions, including the use of dot and cross diagrams
refs.1.22: Recall that an ion is an atom or group of atoms with a positive or negative charge
refs.1.23: Calculate the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in simple ions given the atomic number and mass number
refs.1.24: Explain the formation of ions in ionic compounds from their atoms, limited to compounds of elements in groups 1, 2, 6 and 7
refs.1.25: Explain the use of the endings –ide and –ate in the names of compounds
refs.1.26: Deduce the formulae of ionic compounds (including oxides, hydroxides, halides, nitrates, carbonates and sulfates) given the formulae of the constituent ions
refs.1.27: Explain the structure of an ionic compound as a lattice structure a consisting of a regular arrangement of ions b held together by strong electrostatic forces (ionic bonds) between oppositely-charged ions
refs.1.28: Explain how a covalent bond is formed when a pair of electrons is shared between two atoms
refs.1.29: Recall that covalent bonding results in the formation of molecules
refs.1.30: Recall the typical size (order of magnitude) of atoms and small molecules
refs.1.31: Explain the formation of simple molecular, covalent substances, using dot and cross diagrams, including: a hydrogen b hydrogen chloride c water d methane e oxygen f carbon dioxide
refs.1.32: Explain why elements and compounds can be classified as: a ionic b simple molecular (covalent) c giant covalent d metallic and how the structure and bonding of these types of substances results in different physical properties, including relative melting point and boiling point, relative solubility in water and ability to conduct electricity (as solids and in solution)
refs.1.33: Explain the properties of ionic compounds limited to: a high melting points and boiling points, in terms of forces between ions b whether or not they conduct electricity as solids, when molten and in aqueous solution
refs.1.34: Explain the properties of typical covalent, simple molecular compounds limited to: a low melting points and boiling points, in terms of forces between molecules (intermolecular forces) b poor conduction of electricity
refs.1.35: Recall that graphite and diamond are different forms of carbon and that they are examples of giant covalent substances
refs.1.36: Describe the structures of graphite and diamond
refs.1.37: Explain, in terms of structure and bonding, why graphite is used to make electrodes and as a lubricant, whereas diamond is used in cutting tools
refs.1.38: Explain the properties of fullerenes including C and graphene in terms of their structures and bonding
refs.1.39: Describe, using poly(ethene) as the example, that simple polymers consist of large molecules containing chains of carbon atoms
refs.1.40: Explain the properties of metals, including malleability and the ability to conduct electricity
refs.1.41: Describe the limitations of particular representations and models, to include dot and cross, ball and stick models and two- and three-dimensional representations
refs.1.42: Describe most metals as shiny solids which have high melting points, high density and are good conductors of electricity whereas most non-metals have low boiling points and are poor conductors of electricity
refs.1.43: Calculate: a relative formula mass given relative atomic masses b percentage by mass of an element in a compound given relative atomic masses
refs.1.44: Calculate the formulae of simple compounds from reacting masses or percentage composition and understand that these are empirical formulae
refs.1.45: Deduce: a the empirical formula of a compound from the formula of its molecule b the molecular formula of a compound from its empirical formula and its relative molecular mass
refs.1.46: Describe an experiment to determine the empirical formula of a simple compound such as magnesium oxide
refs.1.47: Explain the law of conservation of mass applied to: a a closed system including a precipitation reaction in a closed flask b a non-enclosed system including a reaction in an open flask that takes in or gives out a gas
refs.1.48: Calculate masses of reactants and products from balanced equations, given the mass of one substance
refs.1.49: Calculate the concentration of solutions in g dm
refs.1.50: Recall that one mole of particles of a substance is defined as: a the Avogadro constant number of particles (6.02 × 10 atoms, molecules, formulae or ions) of that substance b a mass of ‘relative particle mass’ g 16
refs.1.51: Calculate the number of: a moles of particles of a substance in a given mass of that substance and vice versa b particles of a substance in a given number of moles of that substance and vice versa c particles of a substance in a given mass of that substance and vice versa
refs.1.52: Explain why, in a reaction, the mass of product formed is controlled by the mass of the reactant which is not in excess
refs.1.53: Deduce the stoichiometry of a reaction from the masses of the reactants and products
refs.2.1: Describe the arrangement, movement and the relative energy of particles in each of the three states of matter: solid, liquid and gas
refs.2.2: Recall the names used for the interconversions between the three states of matter, recognising that these are physical changes: contrasted with chemical reactions that result in chemical changes
refs.2.3: Explain the changes in arrangement, movement and energy of particles during these interconversions
refs.2.4: Predict the physical state of a substance under specified conditions, given suitable data
refs.2.5: Explain the difference between the use of ‘pure’ in chemistry compared with its everyday use and the differences in chemistry between a pure substance and a mixture
refs.2.6: Interpret melting point data to distinguish between pure substances which have a sharp melting point and mixtures which melt over a range of temperatures
refs.2.7: Explain the types of mixtures that can be separated by using the following experimental techniques: a simple distillation b fractional distillation c filtration d crystallisation e paper chromatography
refs.2.8: Describe an appropriate experimental technique to separate a mixture, knowing the properties of the components of the mixture 18
refs.2.9: Describe paper chromatography as the separation of mixtures of soluble substances by running a solvent (mobile phase) through the mixture on the paper (the paper contains the stationary phase), which causes the substances to move at different rates over the paper
refs.2.10: Interpret a paper chromatogram: a to distinguish between pure and impure substances b to identify substances by comparison with known substances c to identify substances by calculation and use of R values
refs.2.11: Investigate the composition of inks using simple distillation and paper chromatography
refs.2.12: Describe how: a waste and ground water can be made potable, including the need for sedimentation, filtration and chlorination b sea water can be made potable by using distillation c water used in analysis must not contain any dissolved salts
refs.3.1: Recall that acids in solution are sources of hydrogen ions and alkalis in solution are sources of hydroxide ions
refs.3.2: Recall that a neutral solution has a pH of 7 and that acidic solutions have lower pH values and alkaline solutions higher pH values
refs.3.3: Recall the effect of acids and alkalis on indicators, including litmus, methyl orange and phenolphthalein
refs.3.4: Recall that the higher the concentration of hydrogen ions in an acidic solution, the lower the pH; and the higher the concentration of hydroxide ions in an alkaline solution, the higher the pH

refs.3.6: powdered calcium hydroxide or calcium oxide to a fixed volume of dilute hydrochloric acid
refs.3.7: Explain the terms dilute and concentrated, with respect to amount of substances in solution
refs.3.8: Explain the terms weak and strong acids, with respect to the degree of dissociation into ions
refs.3.9: Recall that a base is any substance that reacts with an acid to form a salt and water only
refs.3.10: Recall that alkalis are soluble bases
refs.3.11: Explain the general reactions of aqueous solutions of acids with: a metals b metal oxides c metal hydroxides d metal carbonates to produce salts
refs.3.12: Describe the chemical test for: a hydrogen b carbon dioxide (using limewater)
refs.3.13: Describe a neutralisation reaction as a reaction between an acid and a base
refs.3.14: Explain an acid-alkali neutralisation as a reaction in which hydrogen ions (H ) from the acid react with hydroxide ions (OH ) from the alkali to form water 20
refs.3.15: Explain why, if soluble salts are prepared from an acid and an insoluble reactant: a excess of the reactant is added b the excess reactant is removed c the solution remaining is only salt and water
refs.3.16: Explain why, if soluble salts are prepared from an acid and a soluble reactant: a titration must be used b the acid and the soluble reactant are then mixed in the correct proportions c the solution remaining, after reaction, is only salt and water
refs.3.17: Investigate the preparation of pure, dry hydrated copper sulfate crystals starting from copper oxide including the use of a water bath
refs.3.18: Describe how to carry out an acid-alkali titration, using burette, pipette and a suitable indicator, to prepare a pure, dry salt
refs.3.19: Recall the general rules which describe the solubility of common types of substances in water: a all common sodium, potassium and ammonium salts are soluble b all nitrates are soluble c common chlorides are soluble except those of silver and lead d common sulfates are soluble except those of lead, barium and calcium e common carbonates and hydroxides are insoluble except those of sodium, potassium and ammonium
refs.3.20: Predict, using solubility rules, whether or not a precipitate will be formed when named solutions are mixed together, naming the precipitate if any
refs.3.21: Describe the method used to prepare a pure, dry sample of an insoluble salt
refs.3.22: Recall that electrolytes are ionic compounds in the molten state or dissolved in water
refs.3.23: Describe electrolysis as a process in which electrical energy, from a direct current supply, decomposes electrolytes
refs.3.24: Explain the movement of ions during electrolysis, in which: a positively charged cations migrate to the negatively charged cathode b negatively charged anions migrate to the positively charged anode
refs.3.25: Explain the formation of the products in the electrolysis, using inert electrodes, of some electrolytes, including: a copper chloride solution b sodium chloride solution c sodium sulfate solution d water acidified with sulfuric acid e molten lead bromide (demonstration)
refs.3.26: Predict the products of electrolysis of other binary, ionic compounds in the molten state
refs.3.27: Write half equations for reactions occurring at the anode and cathode in electrolysis
refs.3.28: Explain oxidation and reduction in terms of loss or gain of electrons
refs.3.29: Recall that reduction occurs at the cathode and that oxidation occurs at the anode in electrolysis reactions
refs.3.30: Explain the formation of the products in the electrolysis of copper sulfate solution, using copper electrodes, and how this electrolysis can be used to purify copper
refs.3.31: Investigate the electrolysis of copper sulfate solution with inert electrodes and copper electrodes
refs.4.1: Deduce the relative reactivity of some metals, by their reactions with water, acids and salt solutions
refs.4.2: Explain displacement reactions as redox reactions, in terms of gain or loss of electrons
refs.4.3: Explain the reactivity series of metals (potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, (carbon), zinc, iron, (hydrogen), copper, silver, gold) in terms of the reactivity of the metals with water and dilute acids and that these reactions show the relative tendency of metal atoms to form cations
refs.4.4: Recall that: a most metals are extracted from ores found in the Earth’s crust b unreactive metals are found in the Earth’s crust as the uncombined elements
refs.4.5: Explain oxidation as the gain of oxygen and reduction as the loss of oxygen
refs.4.6: Recall that the extraction of metals involves reduction of ores
refs.4.7: Explain why the method used to extract a metal from its ore is related to its position in the reactivity series and the cost of the extraction process, illustrated by a heating with carbon (including iron) b electrolysis (including aluminium) (knowledge of the blast furnace is not required)
refs.4.8: Evaluate alternative biological methods of metal extraction (bacterial and phytoextraction)
refs.4.9: Explain how a metal’s relative resistance to oxidation is related to its position in the reactivity series
refs.4.10: Evaluate the advantages of recycling metals, including economic implications and how recycling can preserve both the environment and the supply of valuable raw materials
refs.4.11: Describe that a life-cycle assessment for a product involves consideration of the effect on the environment of obtaining the raw materials, manufacturing the product, using the product and disposing of the product when it is no longer useful
refs.4.12: Evaluate data from a life cycle assessment of a product
refs.4.13: Recall that chemical reactions are reversible, the use of the symbol ⇌ in equations and that the direction of some reversible reactions can be altered by changing the reaction conditions
refs.4.14: Explain what is meant by dynamic equilibrium
refs.4.15: Describe the formation of ammonia as a reversible reaction between nitrogen (extracted from the air) and hydrogen (obtained from natural gas) and that it can reach a dynamic equilibrium
refs.4.16: Recall the conditions for the Haber process as: a temperature 450 °C b pressure 200 atmospheres c iron catalyst
refs.4.17: Predict how the position of a dynamic equilibrium is affected by changes in: a temperature b pressure c concentration
refs.5.1C: Recall that most metals are transition metals and that their typical properties include: a high melting point b high density c the formation of coloured compounds d catalytic activity of the metals and their compounds as exemplified by iron
refs.5.2C: Recall that the oxidation of metals results in corrosion
refs.5.3C: Explain how rusting of iron can be prevented by: a exclusion of oxygen b exclusion of water c sacrificial protection
refs.5.4C: Explain how electroplating can be used to improve the appearance and/or the resistance to corrosion of metal objects
refs.5.5C: Explain, using models, why converting pure metals into alloys often increases the strength of the product
refs.5.6C: Explain why iron is alloyed with other metals to produce alloy steels
refs.5.7C: Explain how the uses of metals are related to their properties (and vice versa), including aluminium, copper and gold and their alloys including magnalium and brass
refs.5.8C: Calculate the concentration of solutions in mol dm and convert concentration in g dm into mol dm and vice versa
refs.5.9C: Carry out an accurate acid-alkali titration, using burette, pipette and a suitable indicator
refs.5.10C: Carry out simple calculations using the results of titrations to calculate an unknown concentration of a solution or an unknown volume of solution required
refs.5.11C: Calculate the percentage yield of a reaction from the actual yield and the theoretical yield
refs.5.12C: Describe that the actual yield of a reaction is usually less than the theoretical yield and that the causes of this include: a incomplete reactions b practical losses during the experiment c competing, unwanted reactions (side reactions)
refs.5.13C: Recall the atom economy of a reaction forming a desired product
refs.5.14C: Calculate the atom economy of a reaction forming a desired product
refs.5.15C: Explain why a particular reaction pathway is chosen to produce a specified product, given appropriate data such as atom economy, yield, rate, equilibrium position and usefulness of by-products
refs.5.16C: Describe the molar volume, of any gas at room temperature and pressure, as the volume occupied by one mole of molecules of any gas at room temperature and pressure (The molar volume will be provided as 24 dm or 24000 cm in calculations where it is required)
refs.5.17C: Use the molar volume and balanced equations in calculations involving the masses of solids and volumes of gases
refs.5.18C: Use Avogadro’s law to calculate volumes of gases involved in a gaseous reaction, given the relevant equation 26

refs.5.22C: Recall that fertilisers may contain nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium compounds to promote plant growth
refs.5.23C: Describe how ammonia reacts with nitric acid to produce a salt that is used as a fertiliser
refs.5.24C: Describe and compare: a the laboratory preparation of ammonium sulfate from ammonia solution and dilute sulfuric acid on a small scale b the industrial production of ammonium sulfate, used as a fertiliser, in which several stages are required to produce ammonia and sulfuric acid from their raw materials and the production is carried out on a much larger scale (details of the industrial production of sulfuric acid are not required)
refs.5.25C: Recall that a chemical cell produces a voltage until one of the reactants is used up
refs.5.26C: Recall that in a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell hydrogen and oxygen are used to produce a voltage and water is the only product
refs.5.27C: Evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of fuel cells for given uses 28
refs.6.1: Explain why some elements can be classified as alkali metals (group 1), halogens (group 7) or noble gases (group 0), based on their position in the periodic table
refs.6.2: Recall that alkali metals: a are soft b have relatively low melting points
refs.6.3: Describe the reactions of lithium, sodium and potassium with water

refs.6.5: Explain this pattern in reactivity in terms of electronic configurations
refs.6.6: Recall the colours and physical states of chlorine, bromine and iodine at room temperature

refs.6.8: Describe the chemical test for chlorine

refs.6.13: Explain the relative reactivity of the halogens in terms of electronic configurations

refs.6.15: Explain how the uses of noble gases depend on their inertness, low density and/or non-flammability

refs.7.1: conditions of a reaction on the rates of chemical reactions by: a measuring the production of a gas (in the reaction between hydrochloric acid and marble chips) b observing a colour change (in the reaction between sodium thiosulfate and hydrochloric acid)
refs.7.2: Suggest practical methods for determining the rate of a given reaction
refs.7.3: Explain how reactions occur when particles collide and that rates of reaction are increased when the frequency and/or energy of collisions is increased
refs.7.4: Explain the effects on rates of reaction of changes in temperature, concentration, surface area to volume ratio of a solid and pressure (on reactions involving gases) in terms of frequency and/or energy of collisions between particles
refs.7.5: Interpret graphs of mass, volume or concentration of reactant or product against time
refs.7.6: Describe a catalyst as a substance that speeds up the rate of a reaction without altering the products of the reaction, being itself unchanged chemically and in mass at the end of the reaction
refs.7.7: Explain how the addition of a catalyst increases the rate of a reaction in terms of activation energy

refs.7.9: Recall that changes in heat energy accompany the following changes: a salts dissolving in water b neutralisation reactions c displacement reactions d precipitation reactions and that, when these reactions take place in solution, temperature changes can be measured to reflect the heat changes

refs.7.11: Describe an endothermic change or reaction as one in which heat energy is taken in
refs.7.12: Recall that the breaking of bonds is endothermic and the making of bonds is exothermic
refs.7.13: Recall that the overall heat energy change for a reaction is: a exothermic if more heat energy is released in forming bonds in the products than is required in breaking bonds in the reactants b endothermic if less heat energy is released in forming bonds in the products than is required in breaking bonds in the reactants
refs.7.14: Calculate the energy change in a reaction given the energies of bonds (in kJ mol )
refs.7.16: Draw and label reaction profiles for endothermic and exothermic reactions, identifying activation energy
refs.8.1: Recall that hydrocarbons are compounds that contain carbon and hydrogen only
refs.8.2: Describe crude oil as: a a complex mixture of hydrocarbons b containing molecules in which carbon atoms are in chains or rings (names, formulae and structures of specific ring molecules not required) c an important source of useful substances (fuels and feedstock for the petrochemical industry) d a finite resource
refs.8.3: Describe and explain the separation of crude oil into simpler, more useful mixtures by the process of fractional distillation

refs.8.14: Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of using hydrogen, rather than petrol, as a fuel in cars
refs.8.15: Recall that petrol, kerosene and diesel oil are non-renewable fossil fuels obtained from crude oil and methane is a non- renewable fossil fuel found in natural gas
refs.8.16: Explain how cracking involves the breaking down of larger, saturated hydrocarbon molecules (alkanes) into smaller, more useful ones, some of which are unsaturated (alkenes)
refs.8.18: Recall that the gases produced by volcanic activity formed the Earth’s early atmosphere
refs.8.19: Describe that the Earth’s early atmosphere was thought to contain: a little or no oxygen b a large amount of carbon dioxide c water vapour d small amounts of other gases and interpret evidence relating to this

refs.8.23: Describe the chemical test for oxygen
